claim: DGSD has its own mandatory medical leave. Initiation: recommendation of the director of Yale Health or the chief of Mental Health and Counseling; decider: the dean of the School. Three grounds only: danger to self or others; serious disruption of residential/academic communities; refusal to cooperate with the assessment. Individualized assessment of risk and of reasonable modifications (not diagnosis-based). The program chair has no stated role (unlike voluntary medical leave, which needs chair + dean).
quote: The School reserves the right to place a student on a mandatory medical leave of absence when, on recommendation of the director of Yale Health or the chief of the Mental Health and Counseling department, the dean of the School determines that, because of a medical condition, the student is a danger to self or others, the student has seriously disrupted others in the student's residential or academic communities, or the student has refused to cooperate with efforts deemed necessary by Yale Health and the dean to make such determinations. Each case will be assessed individually based on all relevant factors, including, but not limited to, the level of risk presented and the availability of reasonable modifications. Reasonable modifications do not include fundamental alterations to the student's academic, residential, or other relevant communities or programs; in addition, reasonable modifications do not include those that unduly burden university resources.
source: DGSD Bulletin 2026-2027 (Bulletin of Yale University); printed page numbers (PDF page = printed + 2)
appliesTo: DGSD students (all programs, incl. M.F.A. Acting)
uncertainty: Refines the existing entry: the individualized-assessment and reasonable-modification sentences were not quoted before. No separate Yale-wide graduate/professional policy was found; Yale College's 2022 reformed policy does not apply to DGSD.
suggestedSimplification: Trigger only from a Yale Health recommendation event; dean decides; require a risk check with a "modification available?" branch before imposing.

The emergency suspension will not be imposed prior to an opportunity for the student to respond unless circumstances warrant immediate action for the safety and security of members of the community.

suggestedSimplification: Game: mandatory leave takes effect on the dean's decision; the only student action is the after-the-fact appeal.

source: DGSD Bulletin 2026-2027 (Bulletin of Yale University); printed page numbers (PDF page = printed + 2)
uncertainty: Days are not specified as calendar or business days (contrast the disciplinary appeal, which says "five business days", p.156). Treat as calendar days. The same dean who imposed the leave hears the appeal.
suggestedSimplification: Appeal window = 7 calendar days from effective date; single-level; leave stays in force while pending.

claim: End of each term: students not meeting SAP get financial aid warning for the next term (aid continues). Fail again: aid lost unless an appeal succeeds. M.F.A. appeal must include a plan to meet SAP by the end of the following aid term; the Financial Aid Committee decides with the program chair; approval = financial aid probation for one term; an academic plan is required if SAP cannot mathematically be regained in that term. Without appeal, eligibility returns once SAP measures are back in standard.

If the appeal is approved, the student will be placed on financial aid probation and may receive financial aid for the probationary term. An academic plan will be required when the student cannot mathematically regain SAP by the end of the probationary term.

claim: Federal law (July 4, 2025) ended Grad PLUS for new borrowers from July 1, 2026, with a legacy rule for students who borrowed for the same program before that date (three academic years or remainder of program, whichever less, while continuously enrolled). While continuously enrolled in the same program, the student can borrow from the Grad PLUS program for three academic years or the remainder of their program, whichever is less. ... Graduate students in all other programs can borrow up to $20,500 annually, with a lifetime limit of $100,000.
source: Georgetown University Office of Student Financial Services, Key Changes to Federal Student Loans Effective in July 2026 (secondary source)
appliesTo: US federal; affects DGSD domestic borrowers
uncertainty: Secondary source; primary is Pub. L. 119-21 and ED guidance (not fetched).
suggestedSimplification: Entering 2026 cohort: no Grad PLUS; Direct Unsub cap $20,500/yr.

claim: Federally, a leave is not a withdrawal only if it is an approved LOA under 668.22(d), which among other things cannot exceed 180 days in any 12-month period and must let the student complete coursework begun before the leave. A DGSD leave of a full term or more (and with no completion of interrupted courses, p.158) generally will not meet this, so for Title IV it is a withdrawal; withdrawal date for a leave not meeting (d) is the date the leave began.
quote: (d) Approved leave of absence. (1) For purposes of this section (and, for a title IV, HEA program loan borrower, for purposes of terminating the student's in-school status), an institution does not have to treat a leave of absence as a withdrawal if it is an approved leave of absence. ... (vi) The number of days in the approved leave of absence, when added to the number of days in all other approved leaves of absence, does not exceed 180 days in any 12-month period; (vii) Except for a clock-hour or non-term credit hour program ... upon the student's return from the leave of absence, the student is permitted to complete the coursework he or she began prior to the leave of absence ... (vi) If a student takes a leave of absence that does not meet the requirements of paragraph (d) of this section, the date that the student began the leave of absence.
source: 34 CFR 668.22 (eCFR, as amended through 90 FR 504, Jan. 3, 2025)
uncertainty: Whether DGSD classifies its leaves as (d)-approved is not stated; the Bulletin applies R2T4 to "any student who withdraws".
suggestedSimplification: Treat any DGSD leave as a Title IV withdrawal.

(ii) 100 percent, if the student's withdrawal date occurs after (A) Completion of 60 percent ... || (j) Timeframe for the return of title IV funds. claim: An F-1 student whose DSO authorizes withdrawal (which is how a leave is processed in SEVIS) gets 15 days to depart, not 60. The 60-day period is for program completion. A student who drops below full time without DSO approval gets no departure period.

An F-1 student authorized by the DSO to withdraw from classes will be allowed a 15-day period for departure from the United States. However, an F-1 student who fails to maintain a full course of study without the approval of the DSO or otherwise fails to maintain status is not eligible for an additional period for departure.
source: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(iv) (eCFR)

claim: A student returning from leave who was not covered during it gets student Hospitalization/Specialty coverage starting the day dormitories officially open or orientation requires presence; a continuing student enrolled for spring only is covered Feb 1-Jul 31.
quote: For students entering Yale for the first time, readmitted students, and students returning from a leave of absence who have not been covered during their leave, Yale Health Hospitalization & Specialty Care Coverage begins on the day the dormitories officially open or when orientation requires students to be on campus. A continuing student who is enrolled for the fall term only is covered for services from August 1 through January 31; a continuing student enrolled for the spring term only is covered for services from February 1 through July 31.

claim: Military readmits: next term, same enrolled status and academic standing, no repeating completed coursework, prior-year tuition for first year back. Useful as the only explicit readmission mechanics in the Bulletin.
quote: A student who meets all of these conditions will be readmitted for the next term, unless the student requests a later date of readmission. ... Upon returning to the School, the student will resume education without repeating completed course work for courses interrupted by US military service. The student will have the same enrolled status last held and with the same academic standing.
